note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §13.7, Stage 65; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 15) on data/benches/vinegar.json: vinegar and a weak acid's curve. CH3COOH + OH- -> CH3COO- + H2O: the pH rises slowly through the buffer the acid and its salt make, then leaps at the end point (above 7: acetate is a base); at half the end point [HA] = [A-] and pH = pKa (Henderson and Hasselbalch).
title: Experiment: vinegar and a weak acid's curve

report.label: the end point
report.why: The truth is the base that held the flask's acetic acid's moles. Read from the plot, where the pH leaps, near pH 8.7: acetate, the acid's own base, is left at the end point.

report.label: the vinegar's acetic acid
report.why: c = 0.100 x V(end point) / 25.00 mL, times 10 for the dilution. The base's label is 0.100 M; it is 0.0997 (0.040 mol in 401 mL); each pipette delivers within 0.03 mL and the flask holds 250 mL within 0.15.

report.label: acetic acid's pKa
report.why: At half the end point half the acid is its salt, and Henderson and Hasselbalch's pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) is pKa. Its thermodynamic value is 4.76; the pH read there is a little lower, about 4.68, because the ions' activity in a solution of their own strength is less than their concentration (the pH meter reads activity).

steps.title: 25 mL of the vinegar
steps.text: Pick up the pipette and click the vinegar: it draws up to its mark.
steps.why: Vinegar is about 0.8 M: diluted tenfold it takes about 20 mL of a 0.1 M base for 25 mL of it, in the burette's range.

steps.title: Into the volumetric flask
steps.text: Pick up the pipette again and click the volumetric flask: it stands in its neck and runs into it.

checks.text: the pipette on the volumetric flask

steps.title: Until it is empty
steps.text: Wait until the pipette has run out.

steps.title: To the mark
steps.text: Pick up the pipette and click a free square. Then pick up the water bottle, right-click the volumetric flask and click "to the mark".

steps.title: Mixed
steps.text: Right-click the volumetric flask and click "stir", then click 60x on the clock.
steps.why: Water poured on the vinegar lies over it: until it is mixed, what is drawn from the top is weaker than the whole.

steps.title: 25 mL of the diluted
steps.text: Click 1x on the clock. Pick up the pipette and click the volumetric flask: it draws up to its mark. Then pick it up again and click the titration flask.

checks.text: the pipette on the titration flask

steps.title: Until it is empty
steps.text: Wait until the pipette has run out.

steps.title: The pipette away
steps.text: Pick up the pipette and click a free square.

steps.title: Fill the burette
steps.text: Pick up the sodium hydroxide, right-click the burette, type 55 and click "pour". Then pick up the burette and click the titration flask.

steps.title: Log the pH
steps.text: Right-click the titration flask, click "+ pH" under its readings, then open the notebook and click "1 s": it logs the pH every second.

steps.title: Log the burette
steps.text: Close the notebook, right-click the burette, click "+ mL", open the notebook again and click "1 s".

steps.title: A slow stream
steps.text: Close the notebook, right-click the burette, drag its tap to about 15 % and click 60x.

steps.title: Past the end point
steps.text: Watch the pH climb slowly through the buffer, then leap past 11.
steps.why: From the start to near the end the flask holds acetic acid and acetate together, a buffer: the pH moves slowly. When the acid is used up, the next drops of base meet nothing and the pH leaps.

steps.title: Shut it
steps.text: Drag the burette's tap shut. Open the notebook: x the burette's reading, y the pH. The end point is where the curve is steepest; the pKa is the pH at half of it.
